title: Endolymphatic Sac Decompression / Shunt
source_label: Cummings 7e (Surgery for Vestibular Disorders) and Pasha 6e
indications: Definite unilateral Ménière disease with disabling episodic vertigo despite diet, diuretics, and often intratympanic steroids, in a patient who wants to keep hearing and vestibular function. It is the nondestructive surgical step before intratympanic gentamicin or ablative surgery. Vertigo control is reported at about 60 to 80 percent but efficacy is debated given the natural remission of the disease. MRI should exclude a retrocochlear lesion first. The operation is a wide bony decompression of the sac, with or without opening it and placing a shunt into the mastoid.
setup: Supine, head turned; facial nerve monitoring with no long-acting paralysis
Postauricular approach with a standard otologic drill, cutting and diamond burs, and microscope
Gelfoam or silicone sheet ready to block the aditus and keep bone dust out of the middle ear
Silastic sheeting or a shunt tube if the sac is to be opened
Preoperative audiogram and contrast MRI reviewed; laterality confirmed
landmarks: Lateral semicircular canal at the depth of the antrum
Posterior semicircular canal and its dome
Donaldson line (extension of the lateral canal plane bisecting the posterior canal)
Mastoid segment of the facial nerve and digastric ridge
Jugular bulb inferiorly and retrofacial air cells
danger: Mastoid segment of the facial nerve in a poorly pneumatized bone
Posterior fossa dura tear and CSF leak
Bone dust in the middle ear causing ossicular fixation
steps: Confirm the indication

Review that the patient meets criteria for definite Ménière disease on the affected side, that the vertigo is truly episodic and refractory to medical treatment, and that MRI excludes a retrocochlear lesion. Counsel on modest efficacy and the option of intratympanic therapy.
Postauricular exposure
Make a postauricular incision, raise a periosteal flap, and expose the mastoid cortex from the spine of Henle back past the planned position of the sigmoid sinus and down to the mastoid tip.
Cortical mastoidectomy

Perform a complete cortical mastoidectomy, saucerizing the edges. Open the antrum and identify the lateral semicircular canal. Block the aditus with gelfoam and irrigate copiously so bone dust does not enter the middle ear and fix the ossicles.
Identify the posterior canal

Thin the bone over the posterior semicircular canal until its dense otic capsule bone can be seen clearly, without opening it. Draw the Donaldson line mentally from the lateral canal through the posterior canal; the sac always lies below this line.
Follow the facial nerve and digastric ridge

Identify the digastric ridge inferiorly and follow it to the stylomastoid foramen. This locates the mastoid segment of the facial nerve, which forms the anterior-lateral border of the sac area. Open retrofacial air cells if present.
Decompress the sigmoid sinus

Thin and remove bone over the sigmoid sinus and the posterior fossa dura in front of it with a large diamond bur. Decompressing the sinus allows it to be gently retracted and widens access to the presigmoid dura where the sac sits.
Remove the bony plate over the sac

Remove the bone covering the presigmoid posterior fossa dura below the Donaldson line, from the posterior canal back to the sinus and down to the jugular bulb. The sac appears as a thicker, whiter, more vascular area of dura. Follow it anteromedially toward the operculum.
Expose the duct entry

Carefully drill anteromedially through retrofacial cells toward where the duct enters bone medial to the posterior canal, protecting the medial surface of the facial nerve and the posterior canal dome. Wide exposure of the sac is the main goal of the operation.
Decide on a shunt

If the decompression is complete, stop there or open the lateral wall of the sac with a sickle knife and place silastic sheeting into the lumen as a mastoid shunt. Avoid a sac-subarachnoid shunt because of CSF leak risk. If the lumen cannot be found, end with decompression alone.
Close

Remove the aditus block, irrigate the cavity and middle ear entrance, and confirm there is no CSF leak at the dura. Close the periosteal flap and skin in layers and apply a mastoid pressure dressing for 24 hours.
exit_check: Sac widely decompressed below the Donaldson line from the posterior canal to the sigmoid sinus
Posterior canal, facial nerve, and dura intact; no CSF leak
Aditus block removed and middle ear free of bone dust
postop: Outpatient or overnight stay; mastoid dressing for 24 hours
Check facial function and bedside tuning forks
Continue the Ménière diet and medications; audiogram at 6 weeks
Track vertigo frequency with a diary; plan next steps if attacks persist

late: Progressive hearing loss from the disease
Conductive loss from ossicular fixation by bone dust

attending_followup: Define the Donaldson line and explain its role.
A line extended along the plane of the lateral canal that bisects the posterior canal perpendicularly; the endolymphatic sac lies inferior to it, so bone is removed below the line.
What are the boundaries of the endolymphatic sac in the mastoid?
Donaldson line superiorly, sigmoid sinus posteriorly, jugular bulb inferiorly, and the mastoid segment of the facial nerve laterally; the posterior canal lies anterior-superior.
Where does this operation sit in the Ménière treatment ladder?
After lifestyle, diuretics, and intratympanic steroids fail; it is the nondestructive surgical step before intratympanic gentamicin, labyrinthectomy, or vestibular nerve section.
Why is the endolymphatic-subarachnoid shunt rarely used?
It carries higher CSF leak risk and is conceptually flawed because subarachnoid pressure exceeds endolymphatic pressure; mastoid shunt or decompression alone is preferred.
Ménière disease has frequent spontaneous remission, and controlled trials including sham comparisons have shown similar improvement, so benefit may be nonspecific.
